If the tape case has screws holding it together, rather than glue..., then you could do some tape surgery.

Presuming one set of spokes is still good,

wind tape to good end. open tape case.

carefully lift bad spoke wheel and slide tape lock out of wheel.

Get new spoke wheel from blank or other lightly used tape. (Same procedure)

Put tape into dent for tape lock on new wheel. Snap lock into place.

replace wheel and ensure tape follows same path as before.

Reassemble tape case.

If both sets of spokes are bad, some hand winding may be need and a repeat of the above for the second wheel.

If the tape IS glued, break casing (carefully) and put tape into casing of a new blank tape with screws.

Someone may correct the technical terms, but the procedure should be clear enough. This should work, presuming I understood the problem well enough.

7002:
Did you know...

That Astrocade Inc. wanted to encourage more third party software
development?

That even after a series of technical hurdles, and problems raising
the needed capital, the engineers working on the ZGRASS expansion were
willing to do whatever it took to get it released?

That Jay Fenton used to room with Dick Ainsworth, until Dick fell in
love, moved in with his girlfriend, and converted to vegetarianism?

How, might you ask, do I know these things?  Well, it's well known
that I got a large collection of cassette tapes originally belonging
to Arcadian editor Bob Fabris.  I assumed that these had BASIC
programs on them, and many of them do.  But there was also a box
labeled "Audio."  It seems that Bob recorded many Astrocade-related
phone calls and meetings, and these recordings have now passed on to
me.  I've digitized six tapes so far, with it looks like about
twenty-five to go.  (It's hard to say since they're not labeled very
well, and some of the tapes in the Audio box look like programs.)
It's really offering a fascinating window into the history of the
system, something I never would have expected to be preserved.  I've
made some quick notes about the recordings, which I'll upload to give
you guys an idea of what I've found.

Paul

I may upset a few folks, but...
During the time Astrocade was trying to release cartridges, it seemed to me their focus
was on 'deals' (how to get money, how to 'corner the market', who had what role, etc...). I
was not into all the politics, I was into the technology and writing games. There were a
LOT of promises made to a lot of people, very few, if any, were kept. I kept a low profile.
They all wanted to hire me to write more games, but they wanted to pay me in stock,
bonuses later, etc... Not that interesting to someone just getting out of school. So I took
the job at Frederiksen & Shu Labs and worked on early computer/broadcast products and
DMX (Digital Music Express). The last project I did there was a video board for Apple
Computers and that launch my first company, Intelligent Resources.

But, at the time, all I remember was great confusion as to what constituted a good cartridge. And Astrocade had a lot of problems getting folks for programming carts.
Everyone had their favorite idea for a cartridge and every idea was different. No plan, no
strategy, just sort of winging it. I did not like the lack of a plan, so I never signed on...

constant 60fps(and it still drops in some places in the game)
required a pattern board. This is pretty much the same thing
as a blitter processor. The BPA would not do Gorf at 60 FPS
with all those objects on screen.

My point being is the BPA has no hardware assitance outside
of a shift amount and a rotate(that is only valid in hi-res
and therefor eliminates the possibility from the BPA HVGS.)

However everything must be drawn by the z80. There are no sprites,
players, missiles, characters. Its a 4k bit mapped screen and the
z-80 does ALL the work, even in the sound and I/O department.

As wonderful as the Z-80 is, there is only so much you can squeeze
from the Astrocade before it starts to drop frames.

So with all that said, the FPS on an BPA would be possible but is

pull off some 2600 like stuff. Of course, if you had the
memory(like megabytes) you could do what id Software(tm)

Look up tables.

Tons and tons of them. Then you have a snowballs chance
in hell. The tables are pre-computed values that are simply
looked up. This would include 8x8 bit multiplies by writing
two registers and reading two for the 16 bit answer.

What would normally take the a z-80 possibly hundreds of
cycles to perform in software, could be looked up in a matter
of a dozen or so cycles.

This is also the case for any Sin/Cos tan/sqrt functions and
just about anything else you can think of.

This would require memory chips much larger than any practically available back in the day of the BPA. Today that is not an issue.

I can hook up a 1 meg rom to a few unused I/O port addresses of
the BPA and allow full access to that ROM and bigger. No memory
address space would be taken and all sorts of things would become
very possible on the BPA than it could ever hope to do before.

It is pretty much a blitter. It only requires a few bytes
to be output to its control registers. It then does the
operation unassisted by the z80. It has its own address
generators and counters. It does what the z80 would be
doing without the pattern board: writes the data to magic
ram. It performs the draw loop you would normally have the
z80 do. The z80 initiates the draw by writing to the PB's
control registers. The PB then takes over and performs the
draw allowing the z80 to do other things along side the PB.

Though this helps the system a good deal its still not optimal.
Sprite hardware would have been much better.

The z80 and PB share the bus but at least they can BOTH be doing something.

To day, blitters are the way to go as they are so much more
advanced and processors in their own right. The Atari Jaguar
blitter is quite a powerful workhorse. This was ten years after
the BPA and the PB though.

By 'waveform playback' I assumed you meant audio.  Your comment mentions nothing whatsoever about the paddle controllers, so I made the presumption that you were talking about audio.

While we're at it, I believe the paddle controllers work like a 555 oneshot.  At the beginning of a timing interval, the capacitor (C19) connected to the DISCH and MONOS terminals is discharged, then the timing interval begins.  For each pot, the POTL pin of the handle connector is connected to +5 through the I/O chip, and the capacitor charges through the the 6.2 K resistor in series with the POTL connection, and the handle pot back to the POTR handle connection to the capacitor.  At the same time, an internal counter starts to increment.  As soon as the voltage across the capacitor matches an internal reference voltage, the counter contents is latched into the POT register inside the chip, and can be read by the Z80.  Each pot is examined in turn, one at a time.  So without some tricky timing to intercept when the Z80 commands the circuitry to start, your D2A idea may not work.

10 FOR A=0 TO 1000;INPUT B; @(A)=B; NEXT A

Ahh, got it to work.

For future users, here's the "secret".

You must have the files set up as follows:

D:\MESS Emulator\roms\astrocde\astro.bin

Notice that MESS Emulator, roms, astrocde are all just file folders.

Then astro.bin is the file that contains the Astrocade "DNA" or BIOS file.  When you download it off the net you'll get something like:

Astrocade BIOS (1977)(Bally).bin

You've got to change the name to astro.bin and put it into the astrocde file.

THE HELP ON MESS IS WRONG... or very misleading to a beginner.  The way it's written, you'd think the setup would be roms\astro\astro.bin, because below you see coco3\coco3.  See how the file folder name matches the name of the binary file name?  To get it to work, you must have them NOT match.  It's "astrocde" not "astro".  I might as well tell you that the extension is .bin not .rom as well.

QUOTE FROM MESS HELP:

It is recommended to leave these files zipped for neatness' sake, however MESS will also recognize the files if they are extracted to subdirectories, e.g. roms\coco3.zip could be extracted to roms\coco3\coco3.rom and roms\coco3\disk11.rom. Extracting the files into the roms folder itself will not work

END QUOTE

Bally Professional Arcade and Bally Computer System.  Use Bally Professional Arcade.  I'm not sure what the point of Bally Computer System is there.  (Anybody know the difference?)
